title.en: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired: Lugh against Balor
title.zh: 第二次馬格·圖雷德之戰：魯格對巴羅

region.en: Mag Tuired near Eas Dara (Moytirra, Co. Sligo), Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯萊戈郡莫伊蒂拉平原

texts.period: Recorded in Cath Maige Tuired, Leabhar na hUidre (c. 1100) and later MSS; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Two, Chapter III, eBook #14465

summary.en: The whole host of the Fomor lands for the war of the tribute: the Dagda out-eats a cauldron of broth as a delaying spy, each craftsman of the Tuatha vows his miracle — weapons reforged nightly, the dead healed whole by the well of Slaine — and Lugh, kept out of battle by nine guards, breaks loose to drive the red spear through Balor's raised eyelid, burning the Fomorian army with their own king's eye.
summary.zh: 弗摩爾傾族而來爭貢賦之戰：達格達以一釜羹湯延敵且吞之，神族百工各誓其神蹟——夜夜鑄械、斯拉尼井起死回生——魯格為九衛所禁而破陣而出，紅矛貫巴羅啟開之瞼，邪眼向後、以其族之王之眼焚其軍。

sensitivity.note: Battle placed near Eas Dara (Ess Dara) in north Connacht/Sligo per the tale; Moytirra is the traditional identification and a symbolic pin. Location of the tale's second Mag Tuired is debated by scholars.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Dagda went to the Fomor camp to delay them. To make sport of him they filled the king's cauldron with four times twenty gallons of milk and meal and fat, boiled in goats, sheep and pigs, poured it into a hole in the ground, and told him to eat his fill or die; the ladle was big enough for a man and woman to lie in. The Dagda ate until the hole was empty and scraped the gravel with his hand; sleep came on him and the Fomor laughed at his belly, the size of a great house's cauldron; then, heavy as he was, he went home, his dress grotesque, his wheeled fork leaving a track deep enough for a province's boundary ditch. On the way he met the Morrígu washing in the river Unius, one foot on each bank, and she promised him Indech's heart's blood. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lugh called the crafts of Ireland and asked each its help in the battle. Mathgen would throw the twelve chief mountains on the Fomor; the cup-bearers would hide the twelve lochs and twelve rivers from the Fomor but keep drink for Ireland to the end of seven years; Figol would pour three showers of fire on the Fomor and take two-thirds of their strength, while every breath of the men of Ireland would increase their bravery; the witches would enchant trees and stones and sods into an armed host; Carpre the poet would satirize them at sunrise from a hill-top; Goibniu would replace every broken spear and sword for seven years, no point of his missing and no man it touched living again; Credne would supply rivets, hilts, bosses and rims; Luchta the shields and shafts; Diancecht would make whole every man wounded unless head, brain or marrow were cut through. 'Those great things you are boasting, I will do them all with only myself,' said the Dagda. 'It is you are the good god!' they cried, with a great shout of laughter. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Day after day the Fomor wondered: their own dead stayed dead and their broken weapons stayed broken, but the Tuatha's dead came out of the well of Slaine whole and faster than before, for Diancecht and his son and daughter sang spells over it and put herbs in it. Goibniu, Luchta and Credne made spears by three turns and three cuts each. The Fomor sent Ruadan son of Bres and Brigit to spy; he begged a spear-head, a shaft and rivets, and turned and threw the spear at Goibniu, who pulled it out and cast it back through Ruadan.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: Brigit came and keened her son with shrieking and crying; Goibniu went into the well and was healed; but Octriallach had every Fomor throw a stone of the stones of Drinnes into the well of Slaine until it was dried up, and a cairn was raised over it. Nuada and Macha fell by Balor in the battle; then Lugh broke from his nine keepers, and when Balor's men lifted his eyelid with the ivory ring, Lugh's red spear brought the eye out through the back of the head toward his own army, and three times nine of the Fomor died looking at it — and if the eye had not been put out then, the whole of Ireland would have been burned in one flash. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Second Battle of Mag Tuired is the apocalypse of Irish myth — the war in which the gods of craft and light break the tyranny of the sea-peoples, told with an inventory-logic unique in medieval literature: the battle is planned as a division of labor.

The Fomor landed at Scetne, Balor of the Evil Eye at their head with Bres and the Fomorian kings. The Men of Dea determined that Lugh should not enter the battle at all, so great was his death's loss; they left nine men keeping watch on him. The Dagda went to the enemy camp to delay them and was mocked with hospitality: a cauldron of four-and-twenty gallons of milk and meal and fat boiled with goats, sheep and pigs, poured into a pit, and a ladle big enough for a man and a woman to lie in. 'We will make an end of you if you leave any part of it after you.' The Dagda ate until the hole was empty and scraped the gravel with his hand; then he walked home, heavy as he was, in his grotesque cape and horsehide brogues, dragging a wheeled fork that left a track deep enough for a province's boundary ditch — a comic king who is also a boundary-maker. On the road he met the Morrígu washing in the river Unius, one foot on each bank, her hair in nine loosened locks, and she promised him the heart's blood of Indech.

Meanwhile Lugh called the crafts of Ireland and held the war-council as a requirements meeting. Mathgen would throw the twelve mountains on the Fomor; the cup-bearers would hide the twelve lochs and rivers from the Fomor's thirst while drink held for the men of Ireland for seven years; Figol would rain fire on the Fomor and drain their strength while every breath the men of Ireland drew increased it; Bechulle and Dianan would enchant trees and stones and sods into an armed host; Carpre the poet would satirize the Fomor at sunrise from a hill-top with his back to a thorn-tree, a stone and a thorn in his hand; Goibniu would replace every broken weapon for seven years, his spear-points never missing and never leaving life in the man they touched; Credne would supply rivets and hilts and bosses; Luchta the shafts and shields; Diancecht would restore every wounded man unless his head or brain or marrow were gone. 'Those great things you are boasting, I will do them all with only myself,' said the Dagda — and the assembly roared, 'It is you are the good god!'

The battle's secret engine was the well of Slaine, west of the field: Diancecht, his son Octruil and daughter Airmed sang spells over it and filled it with herbs, and the dead brought to it came out whole and quicker than before. Broken weapons were remade nightly at Goibniu's forge, shafts fitted by three cuts. The Fomor sent Ruadan, son of Bres and of Brigit — a grandson of both armies — to spy; he asked for spear-head, shaft and rivets, and threw the finished spear into Goibniu, who pulled it out and cast it back through him. Brigit keened her son with shrieking and crying — the first keening in Ireland, the tale implies. Goibniu was healed in the well; but Octriallach then had every Fomorian throw a stone from the stones of Drinnes into the well of Slaine until it dried and a cairn closed it — the enemy answered resurrection with geology.

On the great day the battle turned against the gods: Nuada of the Silver Hand and Macha fell by Balor, and the Dagda took a dreadful wound from the spear of Ceithlenn, Balor's wife. Then Lugh broke loose from his keepers, ran to the front of the Men of Dea, and sang a song of courage — better to die protecting their country than live in bonds. He and Balor met; Balor called for his eyelid to be lifted with the ring of ivory to see the chatterer; and Lugh's red spear drove the eye out through the back of his grandfather's head, so that it fell upon the Fomorian army and three times nine of them died at the sight of it — for if Lugh had not put out that eye when he did, the whole of Ireland would have been burned in one flash. Indech was crushed in the rout, and the Morrígu, as she had promised, took the full of her two hands of his blood and gave it to the hosts at the ford of Unius, thence called the Ford of Destruction. Bres, taken fleeing, bought his life with the word that pays for Ireland's crops: let the men of Ireland plough, sow and reap on a Tuesday.

The Fomor were beaten to the sea; only four remained, spoilers of corn and milk, till the Morrígu and Angus Og drove them out one Samhain night, that the Fomor might never be over Ireland again. And the Morrígu, standing over the won battle, gave out the victory to the hosts and the rivers and the royal heights of Ireland: 'Peace up to the skies, the skies down to earth, the earth under the skies; strength to every one' — the oldest peace-poem in the island's speech.
narrative.zh: 第二次馬格·圖雷德之戰乃愛爾蘭神話之啟示錄——技藝與光明之神破海上民族之暴政的戰爭，其敘事之獨特在於清單邏輯：戰爭被規劃為一場分工。弗摩爾全族登陸斯克特尼，巴羅為首，布雷斯同行。神族斷定魯格不得參戰（其死損失太大），留九人守之。達格達赴敵營延敵，被以款待嘲弄：一釜四加侖×二十之乳與粉與脂、和羊豬同煮、傾入地坑，勺大可臥男女二人；『汝若食不盡，即死。』達格達食至坑空、以手刮石屑而盡；遂拖重軀而歸，身披怪誕披風、足踏馬皮鞋，持八人方可抬之輪叉，其轍深可為一省界溝——亦是喜劇之王，亦是界線之製造者。途中遇摩里古於尤尼烏斯河中沐浴，一足各踏一岸、九縷散髮垂掛，許以因德赫之心血。魯格則召愛爾蘭百工開戰前會議：馬思根將擲十二大山於敵；司酒者將藏十二湖十二河於敵之渴前，而愛爾蘭之人縱戰七年飲水不竭；菲戈爾將以三場火雨襲敵、削其三分之二勇力，而愛爾蘭之人每一呼吸即增其勇；女巫將咒樹石草皮成軍；詩人卡普雷將於日出時立丘頂、背棘樹、手持石與棘，向敵諷刺；戈伊布尼烏將於七年間每夜補鑄斷劍折矛，其矛不虛發、所觸之人無生；克雷德供鉚釘柄首盾緣；盧克塔供桿盾；迪安徹特能癒一切傷者，除非首、腦、髓已毀。『爾等所誇諸事，我一人可盡為之。』眾大呼：『善神哉！』戰之密機為戰場以西之斯拉尼井：迪安徹特父子與女艾爾梅德詠咒於井、實之以藥，死者入井而出，復原且更疾。破械夜夜重鑄，三切三旋即成一矛。弗摩爾遣魯阿丹（布雷斯與布里吉特之子、兩軍之孫）窺之；借得矛頭、矛桿、鉚釘後，反手擲矛入戈伊布尼烏；鍛神拔矛擲回、貫穿魯阿丹。布里吉特前來哭子——哀歌之始。戈伊布尼烏入井而愈；然奧克特里亞赫令弗摩爾人人自德林內斯取一石投井，直至井涸、冢成——以地質學回應復活。決戰之日形勢轉劣：銀手努阿達與瑪哈死於巴羅之手，達格達中巴羅之妻克思萊恩之矛重傷。魯格破衛而出，直奔陣前，唱勇氣之歌：寧為護國而死，不為苟活於貢賦之下。二人相對；巴羅令以象牙環啟瞼以觀饒舌者；魯格之紅矛貫穿祖父之頭顱後側，眼落敵陣，三九二十七人見之而死——若非當時射出此眼，全愛爾蘭將於一瞬焚盡。因德赫殁於敗陣；摩里古如前所諾，雙手捧其血予尤尼烏斯渡口之眾——自此名毀滅渡口。布雷斯逃而受擒，以一句話買命：令愛爾蘭人於星期二耕、種、收。弗摩爾被逐於海；餘四人損穀毀乳，至一個薩溫之夜為摩里古與安古斯·歐格所逐，弗摩爾永不再凌愛爾蘭。摩里古立於既勝之戰場，向軍眾、河流、王丘宣布勝利：『天上和平，天上之和平及於地，地在天之下；人人得力』——島上語言之最古和平詩。

functions: War as division of labor: the pre-battle council charts every craft's contribution — mythic charter of guilds
Theology of resurrection technology: well of Slaine and nightly reforging against the enemy's geology
Etiology of the ruin-heap and the peace formula: Octriallach's cairn; the Morrígu's 'peace to the skies'
Etiology of the agricultural calendar: Bres's spared life teaching the Tuesday of ploughing, sowing and reaping

title.en: The Dagda's Harp: the Sleeping, Laughing and Crying Tunes
title.zh: 達格達之豎琴：眠曲、笑曲與哭曲

region.en: Fomorian feasting-house after Mag Tuired, north-west Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西北弗摩爾宴屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Recorded in Cath Maige Tuired traditions, 11th c. manuscripts; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Two, Chapter III, eBook #14465

summary.en: After the battle the Fomor carry off the Dagda's harp Uaitne; the Dagda, Lugh and Ogma follow into the feasting-house, call the harp from the wall — 'Come summer, come winter, from the mouth of harps and bags and pipes' — and play the crying tune till the women weep, the laughing tune till children laugh, and the sleepy tune till every Fomorian sleeps, and they walk out through their enemies.
summary.zh: 戰後弗摩爾奪達格達之豎琴瓦伊特尼；達格達偕魯格與歐格瑪追入宴屋，自牆上呼琴——『夏來冬來，自琴囊風袋之口』——奏哭曲使婦人泣、笑曲使孩童笑、眠曲使敵全軍入睡，三人乃自敵陣中從容走出。

sensitivity.note: The three strains (geintrid, goltrid, suantrid) are the canonical classification of Irish music's powers in medieval learning; symbolic pin (an unnamed feasting-house).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lugh and the Dagda and Ogma followed the Fomor after the battle, for they had carried away the Dagda's harp, that was called Uaitne — sometimes Dur-da-Bla, the Oak of Two Blossoms, sometimes Coir-cethar-chuin, the Four-Angled Music. In the feasting-house they found Bres and his father Elathan, and the harp hanging on the wall; and it was in that harp the Dagda had bound the music, so that it would not sound till he called to it. 'Come summer, come winter, from the mouth of harps and bags and pipes,' said the Dagda; and the harp sprang from the wall and came to him, and it killed nine men on its way. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Then he played for them the three things harpers understand: the sleepy tune, and the laughing tune, and the crying tune. When he played the crying tune their tearful women cried; when he played the laughing tune their women and children laughed; when he played the sleepy tune all the hosts fell asleep — and through that sleep the three went away through the Fomor that would have been glad to harm them. And when all was over, the Dagda brought out the heifer he had got for wages from Bres, and at the sound of her call all the cattle of Ireland the Fomor had carried off as tribute were back in their fields again. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Cath Maige Tuired (Stokes 1891)

narrative.en:
Small, comic, and strange, the harp episode is the Irish myth of what music can do to an army — told as a burglary.

After the rout of Mag Tuired, the fleeing Fomor carried off the Dagda's harp, Uaitne — the Four-Angled Music, the Oak of Two Blossoms — and the Dagda went after it with Lugh and Ogma, the three gods walking into the enemy's feasting-house. The harp hung on the wall of the hall where Bres and his father Elathan sat. It had been the Dagda's craft to bind the music into the instrument, so that it would not sound until he called to it; and now he made the call that later harpers kept as a spell of their art: 'Come summer, come winter, from the mouth of harps and bags and pipes.' The harp sprang from the wall and flew to the Dagda's arms, and it killed nine men on its way — music entering the tale as a weapon before it becomes a cure.

Then the Dagda played the three things harpers understand, the canonical three strains of Irish musical learning: the goltraí, the crying tune, at which the tearful women of the hall cried; the gentraí, the laughing tune, at which the women and children laughed; and the suantraí, the sleepy tune, at which the whole Fomorian host fell asleep. Through that sleep the three gods walked out through their enemies, unhindered by men who would have been glad to harm them.

The episode closes with the tale's quietest wonder: the Dagda brought out the black, black-maned heifer he had taken as wages from Bres in the days of rath-building, and at the sound of her call every head of cattle the Fomor had carried away from Ireland as tribute came back to its field. Music had put the enemy to sleep; a cow's voice undid the theft of the land. The tale of the harp thus gathers three cures in one — laughter against grief, sleep against war, and the call of cattle against dispossession — and the Irish harp tradition would keep all three as its charter: the instrument that could make an armed hall laugh, weep, and sleep.
narrative.zh: 短小、滑稽而奇異，豎琴一節乃愛爾蘭之音樂感軍神話——以夜盜之形敘之。馬格·圖雷德潰敗後，弗摩爾奪走達格達之豎琴瓦伊特尼——四角之音、雙花之橡——達格達偕魯格與歐格瑪追之，三神步入敵宴屋。琴懸於布雷斯與其父埃拉塔所在大廳之牆。達格達之技乃將音樂縛於琴身，非其呼喚不鳴；此刻他念出後世琴師奉為咒法之句：『夏來冬來，自琴、袋、風管之口。』琴自牆上躍下、飛入達格達之臂，途中撞死九人——音樂入篇先為武器，後成解藥。達格達遂奏琴師所解之三事，即愛爾蘭樂學之三曲：哭曲（goltraí），滿廳婦人隨之而泣；笑曲（gentraí），婦孺隨之而笑；眠曲（suantraí），弗摩爾全軍入睡。三神自睡敵之中走出，無人能害。一節以最靜之奇觀收束：達格達取出築堡之日自布雷斯處所得傭值之黑鬃母牛，牛鳴一聲，弗摩爾自愛爾蘭奪作貢賦之牛群盡返其野。音樂使敵入睡；牛聲解土地之劫。豎琴之篇故集三療於一——以笑愈悲、以眠息戰、以牛鳴還失——愛爾蘭豎琴傳統後世奉之為其憲章：能使武裝之廳或笑、或泣、或眠之器。

functions: Charter of the three strains: gentraí (joy), goltraí (grief), suantraí (sleep) as music's canonical powers
Etiology of the harp's magic call and of bound-instrument lore among Irish harpers
Restitution myth: the heifer's call restores the tribute-cattle, wealth-return after war
Comic inversion of the war epic: the battle won at last by a lullaby

title.en: The Tuatha Dé Danann Under the Hills: the Feast of Age
title.zh: 達娜之民入山而居：不老之宴

region.en: Sidhe Femen, Co. Offaly, Ireland (Bodb Dearg's seat)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭奧法利郡女神山（波德·德爾格之邸）

texts.period: Recorded in Fenian-cycle framework tales, medieval MSS; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Four, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Beaten by the Sons of the Gael, the Tuatha Dé Danann will not serve them: Manannan finds every beautiful hill of Ireland, hides it with walls no man can see through, and makes the Feast of Age where Goibniu's ale keeps old age away and the pigs killed at evening are alive at morning — the gods become the Sídhe under the raths.
summary.zh: 達娜之民敗於蓋爾人之子而不肯臣服：瑪南南為之擇愛爾蘭最美之丘，以隱形之牆環之，並設不老之宴——戈伊布尼烏之麥酒令人不老不病不死，夕殺之豬晨復為活——諸神遂為塚下之西德族。

sensitivity.note: The settlement under the hills is the charter myth of fairy-fort (rath) respect in living Irish folklore; Sidhe Femen is placed in Offaly near Slieve Bloom in the tale.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Tuatha Dé Danann, after they were beaten, would not go under the sway of the sons of Miled, but went away by themselves. Because Manannan son of Lir understood all enchantments, they left it to him to find places where they would be safe from their enemies; he chose the most beautiful of the hills and valleys of Ireland for them to settle in, and put hidden walls about them that no man could see through, but they themselves could see through them and pass through them. He made the Feast of Age for them, and the ale of Goibniu they drank at it kept whoever tasted it from age and sickness and death; and the swine he gave them, though killed and eaten one day, were alive and fit for eating again the next day, and so on for ever. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Four ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: They said it were better to have one king over them; and the chiefs gathered and gave the kingship to Bodb Dearg son of the Dagda, for his father's sake, his own sake, and because he was the eldest of the Dagda's children. He had his house at Sidhe Femen with great enchantments about it; Cliach the harper played outside it a whole year for his daughter's hand until a lake burst up under his feet. Later three landless sons of a king of Ireland fasted on the Men of Dea at Brugh na Boinn, and were given Midhir's three daughters in marriage with dowers of red gold, clothing, an ever-filling vat, a wine-making horn, swords and spears, a rath, an unfailing cook and a musician whose playing put childbirth-pains to sleep — and apple-trees from Angus, one in bloom, one shedding, one in ripe fruit. narrative.en:
Defeat did not end the Tuatha Dé Danann — it converted them into the hidden people of Ireland, and this settlement is the myth behind every fairy-fort a farmer ever left unploughed.

When the Sons of the Gael had the island, the beaten gods would not go under their sway. They went away by themselves — not out of Ireland, but under it. Manannan son of Lir, who understood all enchantments, was given the task of finding places where they would be safe from their enemies; he chose out the most beautiful of the hills and valleys of Ireland for them to settle in, and put hidden walls about them, so that no man could see through them, but the people of the Sídhe could see through them and pass through them at will. The raths and mounds of the island became doors.

And he made the Feast of Age for them, the coibche of immortality: the ale of Goibniu the smith, that kept whoever tasted it from age and from sickness and from death; and his own swine, that were killed and eaten one day and alive and fit for eating again the next, and so on for ever. Food without decrement — the whole theology of the Sídhe reduced to a larder.

Then politics returned: better one king over them than a scattering through the whole of Ireland. The candidates were Bodb Dearg son of the Dagda, Ilbrech of Ess Ruadh, Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh, Midhir the Proud of Bri Leith, and Angus Og — who alone did not covet the kingship. The chiefs gave it to Bodb Dearg, for his father's sake and his own, being the eldest of the Dagda's children. His house was Sidhe Femen, walled with great enchantments: the harper Cliach played outside it a full year for the hand of a daughter and won nothing until the ground itself burst under his music into a lake on a mountaintop. His swineherd's pig, squealing before it, would mark the inn where blood would be shed — the first omen of Conaire's death at Da Derga's.

The tale also shows the two peoples dealing by covenant rather than war. Three landless king's sons of Ireland — Eochaid, Fiacha and Ruide — fasted on the Tuatha at Brugh na Boinne, the fast being the oldest legal weapon of the weak; and the gods answered it with a marriage-alliance. Midhir's three daughters were given them, with dowers that inventory the Sídhe economy: red gold from fifty king's sons, raiment of all colors, a vat that turned pure water to mead, a horn that turned sea-water to wine, fifty swords and fifty spears of Lir, a rath from Angus, a cook under geis never to refuse food whose store refilled itself, and a musician whose playing would put women in the pangs of childbirth and wounded men to sleep. And Angus bade them carry away three apple-trees from the oak-wood — one in full bloom, one shedding its blossom, one covered in ripe fruit — spring, fall, and harvest to be carried in the hand. The sons of the Gael and the Men of Dea would keep trading: heroes visiting the hills, gods walking out of them, and the Fianna's stories full of both.
narrative.zh: 戰敗並未終結達娜之民——而是將其轉化為愛爾蘭之隱族；此篇即每一個農人從不犁耕之仙堡（rath）背後之神話。蓋爾人既得全島，敗北之神不肯臣服，遂自去——非出島，而是入島之下。通曉一切咒法之瑪南南受命擇地：於愛爾蘭最美之丘谷中為其民定居，並環以隱形之牆——人不能透視，西德之民卻能透牆出入自便。島上塚丘從此為門。又為之設『不老之宴』：戈伊布尼烏鍛神之麥酒，飲者不老不病不死；瑪南南之豬，夕殺晨活、日日可食、永不匱乏——食物無減量，西德神學盡在食櫥之中。隨後政治復歸：與其散居全島，不如一王統之。候選者：達格達之子波德·德爾格、埃斯·魯阿赫之伊爾布雷克、白野之丘裡爾、驕傲之米迪爾（布里·萊斯）、與安古斯·歐格——惟彼不慕王位。眾以其父之故、其自身之故、且為達格達長子，立波德·德爾格為王。其邸為女神山（Sidhe Femen），咒牆環繞：琴師克利亞赫為求其女之手在牆外彈琴一整年而不得入，直至其樂使足下山體迸裂成湖。其牧豬人之豬嘶鳴之處，必有流血之宴——達·德爾格客棧中科奈雷之死的初兆。故事亦示兩族以盟約而非戰爭相處：愛爾蘭無地之三王之子（伊奧凱、菲亞赫、魯伊德）於博因堡齋戒以迫神族——齋戒乃弱者最古之法器；神族以聯姻答之。米迪爾三女下嫁，嫁妝盤點西德經濟：五十王之子之赤金、五彩衣、化淨水為蜜酒之甕、化海水為酒之角、裡爾之五十劍五十矛、安古斯之堡、受geis約束永不拒食且食盡自續之庖婦、能令產婦與傷者入睡之樂師；安古斯又令攜走橡林三株蘋果樹——一株盛花、一株落英、一株結實——春分、秋分、收穫，皆可握於掌中。蓋爾人之子與達娜之民自此往來不絕：英雄訪丘、神靈出丘，費恩納之故事中兩者皆滿。

title.en: The Morrígu Washes at the Ford of Unius
title.zh: 摩里古於尤尼烏斯渡口沐浴

region.zh: 愛爾蘭斯萊戈郡尤尼烏斯河（今昂欣河）

texts.period: Recorded in Cath Maige Tuired, 11th c.; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Two, Chapter III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Sent to spy on the Fomorian camp, the Dagda meets the Morrígu bathing in the river Unius, one foot on each bank, her hair in nine loosened locks, and they couple — the sacred marriage before battle; she promises to take the heart's blood of Indech, and after the war she brings the full of her two hands of it to the hosts at the ford, thence called the Ford of Destruction.
summary.zh: 達格達奉命窺弗摩爾營，於尤尼烏斯河遇摩里古沐浴——一足各踏一岸、九縷散髮垂掛——二人結合，即戰前聖婚；彼誓取因德赫之心血，戰後於渡口以雙手捧血予軍眾——渡口自此名毀滅渡口。

sensitivity.note: The ritual coupling of the Dagda and the Morrígu before battle is a documented hieros gamos in Cath Maige Tuired; handled as mythology, not erotica, from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Lugh sent the Dagda to spy out the Fomor and delay them; the Dagda ate their mockery-cauldron of broth to the last scraping and slept and went home, grotesque and heavy. And on his way he saw the Battle-Crow, the Morrígu, washing herself in the river Unius of Connacht, one of her two feet at Ullad Echne to the south of the water and the other at Loscuinn to the north, and her hair hanging in nine loosened locks. And she said to the Dagda that she would bring the heart's blood of Indech, son of De Domnann, that had threatened him, to the men of Ireland. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: In the battle Indech fell and was crushed, and blood burst from his mouth; and then the Morrígu came into the battle, and she was heartening the Tuatha Dé Danann to fight well; and as she had promised the Dagda, she took the full of her two hands of Indech's blood and gave it to the armies that were waiting at the ford of Unius; and it was called the Ford of Destruction from that day. After the victory she proclaimed the peace to the hosts and the rivers and the royal heights of Ireland: 'Peace up to the skies, the skies down to earth, the earth under the skies; strength to every one.' Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
Between the porridge and the killing, the Second Battle keeps one scene that medievalists have called the strangest in Irish myth: the Dagda's rendezvous with the Morrígu at the river.

The Dagda, sent to spy out the Fomor camp and delay them, had eaten their mocking broth to the scraped gravel and dragged himself home in his grotesque finery. On his way he saw the Battle-Crow, the Morrígu, washing in the river Unius of Connacht — one of her two feet at Ullad Echne, south of the water, the other at Loscuinn, north of it, her hair hanging in nine loosened locks. In the older tale the sight is frank and ritual: the war-goddess at her bath meets the god of abundance, and they couple; the union before battle is the sacred marriage of Ireland — the land's power to give victory renewed by the meeting of its two oldest divine powers, the raven of war and the good god of plenty. In Gregory's retelling the meeting is condensed to the promise: the Morrígu tells the Dagda she will bring the heart's blood of Indech, son of De Domnann, who had threatened him, to the men of Ireland.

She keeps it. In the battle Indech falls, crushed, blood bursting from his mouth; and the Morrígu comes into the fight, heartening the Tuatha Dé to battle, and takes the full of her two hands of Indech's blood and gives it to the armies waiting at the ford of Unius — the ford called the Ford of Destruction from that day. The blood of the enemy king is the beverage of victory: a rite enacted in story rather than in any attested cult, but shaped exactly like one.

And after the killing is over, the same goddess — who stirs wars, who flies as a crow over battlefields, who turned a woman into a pool of water for following her — gives out the news of the great victory to the hosts and to the royal heights of Ireland and to its chief rivers and its river-mouths, in the words every later battle-piece in Irish echoes: 'Peace up to the skies, the skies down to earth, the earth under the skies; strength to every one.' The terrible queen is the one who announces peace; the poem that closes the war is hers. In the iconography of the tale, sovereignty is not a gentle maiden but a washer at the ford — and she decides who wins it.
narrative.zh: 在羹湯與殺戮之間，第二次大戰保存了愛爾蘭神話中最為奇異之一幕：達格達與摩里古於河畔之約。達格達奉命窺敵營、延敵勢，食盡嘲弄之羹至刮盡石屑，拖怪誕之裝而歸。途中見戰烏摩里古於康諾特尤尼烏斯河沐浴——一足踏南岸烏拉德·埃赫內，一足踏北岸洛斯昆，九縷散髮垂掛。古篇所述直率而具儀式性：戰烏於浴中遇豐足之神，二人結合；戰前之結合即愛爾蘭之聖婚——以戰鴉與善神二族最古老神力之會，更新土地賜勝之權。格雷戈里之重述將相會濃縮為一句誓言：摩里古告達格達，她將把威脅過他的因德赫（德·多姆南之子）之心血帶給愛爾蘭之人。她守約。戰中因德赫被碾碎而死，血自口迸；摩里古入戰陣、激勵神族奮戰，並如前諾，雙手捧滿因德赫之血，賜予等候於尤尼烏斯渡口之軍眾——渡口自此名毀滅渡口。敵王之血即勝利之飲：此為以故事形式展演之儀式，形制與祭祀無異。殺戮既畢，同一女神——曾挑動戰爭、曾化鴉臨陣、曾令隨行者化為水泊——向軍眾、王丘、河流與河口宣布大捷，其辭為後世愛爾蘭戰歌所呼應：『天上和平，天上之和平及於地，地在天之下；人人得力。』可怖之后即是宣布和平者；戰後之詩出於其口。故事之圖像學如是：主權非溫柔少女，而為渡口浣衣者——而誰得之，由她決定。

title.en: Midhir and Etain: the Rebirth at the Golden Cup
title.zh: 米迪爾與艾塔恩：金杯中之重生

region.en: Bri Leith (Slieve Calry, Co. Longford), Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭朗福德郡布里·萊斯山

texts.period: Recorded as Tochmarc Étaíne, medieval Irish MSS (Lebor na hUidre and Book of Leinster); Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Four, Chapter VII, eBook #14465

summary.en: The jealous Fuamach turns Midhir's new wife Etain into a fly; blown through Ireland for seven years, the fly falls into the golden cup of Etar's wife and is swallowed — and born again as a king's daughter, wooed by the High King Eochaid and reclaimed at last by Midhir, who wins a chess game, lifts her through the roof of Tara as two swans linked by a chain of gold, and names the Hill of Cruachan for his maid.
summary.zh: 妒婦富馬赫以咒化米迪爾新妻艾塔恩為蠅；蠅隨風飄蕩愛爾蘭七年，終墜入埃塔爾之妻金杯而飲——轉生為王女；受至高王伊奧凱迪求娶，終為米迪爾復得——彼以棋勝、自塔拉屋頂抱之而出，化雙鵠以金鏈相連，並以其侍女之名命名克魯亨山。

sensitivity.note: Etain's rebirth through the drinking-vessel is the classic Irish rebirth motif; handled as mythology from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Midhir the Proud took Etain Echraide to wife, and there was great jealousy on Fuamach his first wife; with the druid Bresal Etarlaim's spells she drove Etain out of Bri Leith. Angus Og took Etain into his keeping and made a sunny house for her everywhere they rested, with invisible walls; but Fuamach, finding Etain alone, turned her with druid spells into a fly and sent a blast of wind through the window that swept her away. Angus struck Fuamach's head off when he found her with the druid. For seven years the fly was blown to and fro through Ireland, until she fell from a roof-beam into the golden cup beside Etar's wife at a feast, and was drunk down with the wine — and at the end of nine months she was born again as Etar's daughter. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Four ch. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Midhir found her grown, and said to her, 'Come with me to the wonderful country that is mine... The young never grow old there.' 'Will you come if Eochaid gives you leave?' Etain said she would do that. So Midhir came to Tara and won the first two games of chess, paying fifty brown horses and hard works of clearing and planting; in the third game he won and asked Etain, and would take only a kiss. At the month's end, with all the doors shut and armed men ready, Midhir took Etain in his right arm, rose up through the roof of the palace, and the pursuers saw only two swans high in the air, linked by a chain of gold. Serving in his hill later, Etain's maid was told her own name would be put on the place — the Hill of Cruachan. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The wooing of Etain is the great Irish tale of identity worn like clothing: a woman carried through every shape a druid's rod can give, until the shape that comes out at the end is recognized — by the man who lost her.

Midhir the Proud, one of the five candidates for the kingship of the Sídhe, lived at Bri Leith with his first wife Fuamach and his daughter Bri. When he took Etain Echraide to wife, Fuamach's jealousy called the druid Bresal Etarlaim, whose spells let her drive Etain out. Angus Og sheltered the wanderer, making her a sunny house with invisible walls wherever they rested; but Fuamach came on Etain alone, turned her with druid spells into a fly, and sent a blast of wind through the window that swept her into the world. For that head, Angus would later strike Fuamach's off. The fly was blown to and fro through Ireland for seven years of misery, until one day she fell from a roof-beam into the golden cup that stood beside Etar's wife at a feast; the queen drank her down with the wine — and at the end of nine months Etain was born again, Etar's daughter, named as before.

Midhir found her out and came to her as a stranger riding a bay horse over the plain, and sang to her by the strand of Inver Cechmaine of the battles that would happen for her sake. Then the High King Eochaid saw her at a well, washing her hair with a comb of gold and silver over a basin with four golden birds — purple cloak, green silk, sunlight falling on gold — and loved her and paid the bride-price and brought her to Teamhair. At the feast there, Eochaid's brother Ailell fell in love with her, sickened of it, and wasted a year unable to name his sickness; Etain, tending him, guessed the truth and made the great gesture of the tale — she would heal him by granting his desire, and bade him come at dawn. But a man in Ailell's shape came before him each morning and put Ailell to sleep so that he could not rise: Midhir himself, preventing the wrong by love. On the third morning Etain said to the stranger, 'It is not you at all I come to meet here' — and he answered: 'It would be more fitting for you to come to meet me than any other one. For in the time long ago, I was your first husband.' It was Midhir of Bri Leith, and he confessed that he had put the desire on Ailell and had hindered the meeting, to keep Etain's good name.

The king's consent became the wager. Midhir came to Teamhair with his chessboard of silver and men of gold, lost twice (paying fifty brown horses, making a road over Moin Lamraide, clearing Midhe of stones, covering Tethra with rushes and Darbrech with trees — works that taught Eochaid to yoke oxen by the neck and shoulder and won him his name Airem, of the Plough), then won the third game and asked Etain. 'I will not give her to you,' said the king; a kiss only, at the month's end. When the month was up the doors were shut and armed men crowded the hall; Midhir took Etain in his right arm, rose up through the roof with her, and the host that rushed out saw only two swans high in the air, linked together by a chain of gold. Nine years of siege and digging at Bri Leith could not bring her back until the druid Codal found her with his yew-rod oghams; then Midhir sent out three times twenty women with Etain's own appearance and bade the king choose — the test of desire against knowledge. Eochaid chose first his own daughter; then, called by the true voice, chose Etain, and brought her home. For the insult of digging into a Sídhe hill, the tale says, Midhir's people later brought Conaire, Eochaid's grandson, to his death at Da Derga's Inn: the otherworld keeps its accounts.
narrative.zh: 艾塔恩求婚記乃愛爾蘭之『身分如衣』大故事：一女子被德魯伊之杖化盡百形，直到最後現出之形被認出——由失去她的人。驕傲的米迪爾居布里·萊斯，前妻富馬赫、女布里。娶艾塔恩·埃克雷德後，富馬赫之妒召德魯伊布列薩爾·埃塔爾萊姆，以咒逐艾塔恩出布里·萊斯。安古斯·歐格庇護流浪者，所至之處為其築隱牆之日室；然富馬赫獨遇艾塔恩，以咒化之為蠅、遣風自窗捲入世界。安古斯後斬富馬赫之頭以償。蠅在愛爾蘭飄蕩七年，一夕自屋梁墜入宴會上埃塔爾之妻身旁之金杯，隨酒而飲——九月之後，艾塔恩重生為埃塔爾之女，名字如前。米迪爾尋得其人，跨棗紅馬過平原而來，於因弗·克赫曼尼海灘為其歌頌因她而將至之戰。而至高王伊奧凱迪於井畔見她——金銀梳、四金鳥盆、紫斗篷綠絲衣、日光落於金上——愛之、付聘禮、迎至塔拉。宴上，王弟艾萊爾愛上她、成疾、一年消瘦而不言病因；艾塔恩侍疾、窺破真相，遂行故事之大手筆：許其願以療之，約於黎明。然每晨有形如艾萊爾者先至，使真艾萊爾沉睡不能起——即米迪爾，以愛防止錯誤。第三晨艾塔恩對陌生人曰：『我約之非你。』彼答：『爾當見我更宜。因久遠之前，我乃爾之第一夫。』即布里·萊斯之米迪爾；他承認曾將慾望加於艾萊爾並阻止幽會，以保艾塔恩之名。王之同意遂成賭局。米迪爾攜銀板金子之棋至塔拉，兩負（償五十匹棕馬、修莫因·蘭雷德之路、清米斯之石、以燈心草覆特特拉、以樹覆達布列赫——此工程令伊奧凱迪教民以頸肩架軛，得號『犁者』）；三局勝而求艾塔恩。『不予。』惟一吻，至月終。月圓之夕門戶盡閉、甲士滿堂；米迪爾右臂攜艾塔恩，自屋頂穿出，追者所見惟二鵠高翔、以金鏈相連。布里·萊斯被圍九年、掘山不果，直至德魯伊科達爾以紫杉杖歐甘文尋得其人；米迪爾遣三九二十名同貌之女，令王自擇——慾與知之試。伊奧凱迪先擇己女；聞真聲而後擇艾塔恩，攜之歸。而因掘神丘之辱，故事言：米迪爾之族後使伊奧凱迪之孫科奈雷死於達·德爾格客棧——彼岸自記其帳。

summary.en: Music behind him casts Bran son of Febal asleep; he wakes with a silver blossom-branch in his hand, and a woman in strange clothing sings the otherworld into his desire — no treachery, no death, no sickness in Emhain — and he sails with three nines of men, meets Manannan riding the waves as a flowering plain, lands one man on the Island of Joy, and returns to an Ireland where his voyage is already legend and homecoming is ash.
summary.zh: 身後之樂使費巴爾之子布蘭入睡；醒時手中得銀花之枝；奇裝女子歌彼岸於其心中——艾姆海恩無背信、無死亡、無疾病——遂率三九之人揚帆；遇瑪南南駕浪如花之平原；留一人於歡樂之島；歸時其航已成傳說，登岸者化為灰燼。

sensitivity.note: Symbolic pin: the voyage is westward over the ocean; lat/lon marks a point west of Ireland. The immram genre is a living literary tradition of Irish.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Bran son of Febal, walking near his dun, heard music behind him that kept after him until he fell asleep with the sweetness of the sound; waking, he saw beside him a branch of silver with white blossoms, the whiteness of the silver the same as the whiteness of the blossoms. He carried it into his royal house, and a woman in strange clothing stood among his people and sang the Land of Women to him: a plain where hosts hold games, curraghs racing against chariots on the white silver plain, an old tree with birds calling, no keening and no treachery, nothing hard or rough, only sweet music on the ear; to be without grief, without sorrow, without death, without any sickness, without weakness — that is the sign of Emhain. 'Do not fall upon a bed of sloth; set out on your voyage over the clear sea, and you may chance to come to the Land of Women.' The branch leaped from Bran's hand to hers, and she was gone. Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Bran sailed with three companies of nine. On the sea a man came toward them in a chariot — Manannan son of Lir — singing that what was a clear sea to Bran was a flowery plain to him in his chariot, that what Bran saw as waves he saw as red flowers, the sea-horses bright in summer and a wood of acorns under the boat's head. Bran rounded the Island of Joy, whose crowd laughed and stared without answering, and left one of his own men there, who joined the laughter. At the Land of Women the chief woman threw a ball of thread that held fast in Bran's palm and drew the curragh to land; they dwelt in a house with a bed for every couple, and food on every dish that never came to an end.

narrative.en:
The Voyage of Bran is the founding poem of the Irish immram — the sea-voyage genre that would later carry monks' pious journeys to islands of saints, and it begins not with a ship but with a melody.

Bran son of Febal walked alone near his dun and heard music behind him. It kept after him, however he turned, until the sweetness of the sound put him to sleep; and when he woke there lay beside him a branch of silver with white blossoms, the whiteness of the silver the same as the whiteness of the blossoms. Carrying it into his hall, he found a woman in strange clothing standing among his people, and she sang the otherworld to him in verses that catalog its geography: the plain where the hosts hold their games, curraghs racing chariots on the white silver plain to the south; an old tree in blossom with birds calling from it; no keening and no treachery in the tilled familiar land; nothing hard or rough, only sweet music on the ear; 'to be without grief, without sorrow, without death, without any sickness, without weakness — that is the sign of Emhain.' Then the command that ends all Irish otherworld songs: 'Do not fall upon a bed of sloth; do not be overcome by drunkenness; set out on your voyage over the clear sea, and you may chance to come to the Land of Women.' The branch leaped from Bran's hand back into hers — for he had not the strength to hold it — and she was gone.

He sailed the next morning with three companies of nine. On the second day a man came toward them over the sea in a chariot, and sang to them the relativity of vision: what is a clear sea to Bran in his curragh is a flowery plain to Manannan son of Lir in his chariot; what Bran sees as waves, Manannan sees as red flowers without fault; sea-horses bright in summer; a wood of acorns, gold-leaved, with the smell of wine, under the head of the little boat. Then the islands: first the Island of Joy, where a crowd stared and laughed in gusts and would not talk — Bran set one of his own men ashore, and the man turned to stare at his own ship like a stranger; then the Land of Women, where the chief woman flung a ball of thread that fastened in Bran's palm and drew the curragh in. A house with three-times-nine beds, a bed for every couple, food on every dish that never lessened; and it seemed to them they were a year there.

Then homesickness. Nechtan son of Collbrain begged to go home; the woman of the land warned there would be repentance on it, and gave one law: touch no land when you come to Ireland, and bring the man from the Island of Joy. They came to Srub Bruin; the people on the strand asked who they were, and when Bran said his name they answered, 'We know of no such man, though the voyage of Bran is in our very old stories.' Time on the water had made him a manuscript. Nechtan leaped to the shore — and was a heap of ashes, as if he had lain in the earth for hundreds of years. Bran told the whole story of his wanderings from the beginning to the people, bade them farewell, and sailed; and his wanderings from that time are not known. The voyage that began in music ends in archive: the first immram, and the law of its genre — the otherworld may be visited, but not stepped upon.
narrative.zh: 布蘭遠航乃愛爾蘭imrama（海上航記）文類之奠基詩——後世僧侶將以此文類駛向聖徒之島——而其始非船，乃一曲樂。費巴爾之子布蘭獨行於宅旁，聞身後有樂聲；無論回望，樂聲相隨，至其甜使人眠；醒時身邊有銀花之枝，銀之白與花之白如一。攜枝入廳，見奇裝女子立於族人群中，為其歌彼岸之地理：眾人賽遊之平原、白銀平原上小舟賽戰車、老樹花開群鳥啼鳴、已耕熟悉之地無哀歌無背信、無堅無糙、惟甜樂盈耳；『無憂、無悲、無死、無病、無弱——此即艾姆海恩之徵。』繼以一切彼岸歌之終句：『勿墮懶榻；勿為酒困；啟航於清海之上，或可至女人之地。』花枝自布蘭之手跳回女子之手——他無力持之——女子已杳。翌晨率三九之人啟航。次日海上有人乘戰車而來，歌相對之視界：布蘭小舟下之清海，在瑪南南戰車之下為花之平原；布蘭所見之浪，瑪南南所見為無瑕之紅花；夏日海馬閃亮；小舟首下有橡果之林、金葉含酒香。繼而島嶼：先歡樂之島，人群凝視大笑、不與言語——布蘭留一己之人於岸，其人轉而如陌生人凝視己船；繼至女人之地，主女擲線球、緊粘布蘭掌心，引舟而入。室有三九二十七床，每偶一床，盤中食物永不減少；彼等恍如居一年。然後鄉愁。科爾布萊恩之子內克坦求歸；彼地之女警告必有悔恨，並立法：至愛爾蘭時足勿沾土，且帶回歡樂島上之人。至斯魯布·布魯因；灘上之人問其誰，布蘭自道其名，答曰：『吾等不知此人，然布蘭之航見於吾等甚古之故事。』海上之時已使其成為鈔本。內克坦躍登岸——化為一堆灰燼，如在地中數百年者。布蘭向眾人自始至終講述其漂流，辭別而去；其後漂流無人知曉。始於音樂之航，終於檔案：首篇imram，及其文類之法——彼岸可訪，不可踐踏。

functions: Founding charter of the immram genre: sea-voyage as both heroic quest and (later) monastic pilgrimage
Relativity of vision: one sea, two landscapes — the doctrine that the otherworld is present but unperceived
Taboo of the touched shore: return to time is death — the otherworld's irreversible exchange rate
Lure of the blossom-branch: the sensory token that opens the voyage, template for later vision-tokens

summary.en: A grey-haired stranger with a silver branch of nine golden apples makes a bargain with King Cormac — the branch for three unspecified gifts — then takes his daughter, his son and his wife one by one, until Cormac follows into the misted plain, where a pig boils quarter by quarter as truths are told, and wakes at Tara with his family, the branch, and a cup that breaks under lying words.
summary.zh: 灰髮異客持九枚金蘋果之銀枝與科爾馬克王立約——枝換三件未言之禮——而後一一取其女、其子、其妻；科爾馬克循霧入平原，見豬隨真言而按季熟爛，醒於塔拉，家人、銀枝與一枚謊言之下碎裂之杯皆在其側。

sensitivity.note: The Cup of Truth given to Cormac echoes the judges' ordeal-cups of Irish legal lore; the Well of Knowledge with five streams is Manannan's interpretation of learning.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Cormac, alone in Teamhair, saw an armed man come toward him, quiet, high-looked, grey-haired, with a shining branch on his shoulder that had nine apples of red gold; whoever heard it shaken forgot want and trouble and tiredness. The stranger said he came from a country where there is nothing but truth, and neither age nor withering, heaviness, sadness, jealousy, envy nor pride. Cormac asked for his branch and gave his word for three gifts asked in return. A year later the stranger came for the first gift: Cormac's daughter Aille; a month later his son Carpre Lifecar; then his wife Ethne — and each time Cormac shook the branch and put away the grief of his people in sleep. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Four ch. 11; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Cormac followed through a mist into a plain of duns and marvels — a house thatched with white birds' wings that the wind kept blowing off, a man kindling an oak fire that burned out before he fetched the next, a well with five streams and nine purple hazels over it whose sound was sweeter than any music. In the palace a pig was boiled that never cooked until a truth was told for every quarter of it; the third quarter came with the woman's seven cows and seven sheep; Cormac's own truth — his wife, son and daughter taken and himself following — boiled the whole. His hosts were Manannan and his wife. Cormac woke on the green of Teamhair with his family, the branch, and a gold cup: three lying words under it broke it in three; three true words made it whole again. It was called Cormac's Cup, and it judged between truth and untruth among the Gael until the night of Cormac's death, as Manannan had foretold. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
Ireland's most famous lawgiver-king buys his own judgment, and pays for it with everything he loves — the echtra (adventure) of Cormac is a bargain tale about what wisdom costs.

Cormac, grandson of Conn, sat alone in Teamhair when an armed man came toward him: quiet, high-looked, grey-haired, wearing a shirt ribbed with gold thread and broad shoes of white bronze, and carrying on his shoulder a shining branch with nine apples of red gold. The branch's sound was such that no one on earth could keep in mind any want or trouble or tiredness when it was shaken — forgetfulness as music. Cormac asked where he came from. 'From a country where there is nothing but truth, and where there is neither age nor withering away, nor heaviness, nor sadness, nor jealousy, nor envy, nor pride.' Cormac wanted the branch and the friendship; the stranger set the price: three gifts, unnamed. Cormac promised.

The branch, shaken, put the royal house asleep from that day to the same hour next day. And the gifts came due, one a year or a month apart: 'I will take your daughter, Aille, to-day.' The women of Ireland cried out, and Cormac shook the branch and put their sorrow into sleep. A month later, his son Carpre Lifecar; a night of weeping in Teamhair, silenced by the branch. Then his wife Ethne — and Cormac could not bear it, and followed with all his people into a mist on the Plain of the Wall, and came out alone.

His walk through the plain is a lecture in riddles: a house half-thatched with white birds' wings that the wind blew off as fast as the Riders of the Sídhe laid them on; a man kindling an oak fire that burned out before he could fetch the next tree; then a royal house of bronze beams and silver walls, and on the green a shining well with five streams flowing from it, armies drinking in turn, nine purple hazels of Buan dropping their nuts into the water, five salmon catching them and sending the husks floating down the streams — and the sound of the flowing sweeter than any music men sing.

In the palace sat a man and woman, tall, many-colored; a bath of stones that heated themselves; a host with seven pigs that fed the whole world because each killed pig was alive again tomorrow. A pig was boiled for Cormac — but it never cooked until a truth was told for every quarter of it. The woodsman's truth (an axe that splits its own fuel), the master's truth (a field found ploughed, sowed and reaped, never lessening), the woman's truth (seven cows and seven sheep that feed and clothe the world) — quarter, quarter, quarter. Cormac's truth was the fourth: his wife, son and daughter taken from him, and he following them to that place. With that the whole pig was boiled. The man began to sing, and Cormac slept; he woke to see fifty armed men, his son, his wife and his daughter with them. And there was the gold cup: three lying words spoken under it broke it into three; three true words made it whole. Manannan spoke three true words — that neither wife nor daughter had seen the face of a man since they were taken, that the son had never seen the face of a woman — and the cup became whole; and he gave it to Cormac to judge between truth and untruth among the Gael, with the branch for music. 'And I myself am Manannan, son of Lir, king of the Land of Promise, and I brought you here by enchantments that you might be with me to-night in friendship.' And he read Cormac's riddles for him: the thatchers were the men of art seeking fortune; the fire-kindler the lord more liberal than he can afford; the well the Well of Knowledge, whose five streams are all knowledge's channels — and no one will have knowledge who does not drink from the well or the streams; the people of many arts drink from them all. Cormac woke on the green of Teamhair with his family, the branch and the cup; and the cup was not left in Ireland after the night of Cormac's death, as Manannan had foretold.
narrative.zh: 愛爾蘭最著名之立法者之王買下自己的判斷，而以所愛之一切為價——科爾馬克之歷險（echtra）即一則關於智慧之代價的交易故事。科恩之孫科爾馬克獨坐塔拉，見一甲士前來：沉靜、昂然、灰髮，內穿金線凸紋之衫、足踏白銅闊鞋，肩上負光輝之枝、綴九枚赤金蘋果；枝一搖，世間無人能記住其缺乏、煩惱或倦怠——遺忘即音樂。科爾馬克問其所自。『來自惟有真理之鄉，無老、無衰、無沉重、無悲、無妒、無羨、無傲。』王求其枝與其誼；異客出價：三件禮物，未言其名。王許諾。枝一搖，王宮自當日睡至翌日同時。禮物到期，以年月相隔：『今日我取爾女艾爾。』愛爾蘭婦人哭喊，王搖枝使其悲入眠。一月後其子卡普雷·利菲卡；塔拉泣哭之夜，以枝靜之。繼而其妻埃特尼——王不能堪，率眾循「牆之平原」之霧而追，醒時獨身。其平原之行乃一堂謎語課：半覆白鳥羽之屋，風起即吹散、西德騎者再覆再散；一人焚橡木之火，取次木至而前火已盡；繼而銅梁銀壁之王宮，綠坪上有光井、五源自其中流出，軍隊依次飲水，九株紫色布安榛樹落堅果入水、五鮭接之使殼浮流而下——流水之聲甜於人間任何樂曲。宮中坐高大多彩之一男一女；石自加熱之浴；其主有七豬、可養全世界，因所殺之豬明日復活。為科爾馬克煮一豬——然非每一季有一真言則不熟。樵夫之真（自斷其薪之斧）、主人之真（田自耕自種自收、永不減少）、婦人之真（七牛七羊養活天下）——季、季、季。科爾馬克之真為第四季：其妻、其子、其女被奪，而彼追隨至此。豬乃全熟。主人歌唱使王入睡；醒見五十甲士與其子其妻其女同在。又見金杯：杯下三句謊言，杯碎為三；三句真言，復歸於全。瑪南南說三句真言——妻女被奪以來未見男子之面、其子未見女子之面——杯復全；彼以杯賜科爾馬克，使於蓋爾人中分辨真偽，並留銀枝為樂。『我即瑪南南、裡爾之子、應許之地之王；我以咒法引爾至此，使今夜與我為友。』又為王解其謎：覆羽之匠乃求運之藝人；焚火之漢乃施捨過其力之貴人；井乃知識之井，五流乃知識之諸道——不飲井或流者不得知識；百藝之民飲其全流。科爾馬克醒於塔拉綠坪，家人、枝與杯俱在；而杯如其預言，在科爾馬克死夜之後未留於愛爾蘭。

summary.en: On the Hill of Uisneach a woman invisible to all but the prince Connla calls him to the Land of the Ever-Living Ones; the Druid Coran sings spells to silence her, she throws an apple that feeds Connla for a month without lessening, and when she returns she out-argues both king and Druid — 'where its law comes it scatters the spells on their lips' — until Connla leaps into her shining boat and is never seen again.
summary.zh: 於烏斯內克丘，一女子惟王子科恩拉可見，召之往永生者之地；德魯伊科蘭詠咒禁其聲，彼擲蘋果一枚、足供科恩拉一月之食而不減；女子復至時辯勝王與德魯伊——『其法所至，咒語自散』——科恩拉遂躍入其光輝之舟，永不再見。

sensitivity.note: The apple as otherworld food without decrement parallels Bran's branch and Etain's cup; Uisneach is the mythic navel of Ireland.

Conn heard every word though he saw no one, and called the druid Coran: 'Help me, you that sing spells of the great arts. narrative.en:
The shortest and coldest of the otherworld calls: a king loses his heir not to war but to a sentence of grammar.

Connla of the Red Hair, son of Conn of the Hundred Battles, stood with his father on the Hill of Uisnach — the navel of Ireland — and saw a woman in wonderful clothing. No one saw her but himself. 'I come from Tir-nam-Beo, the Land of the Ever-Living Ones, where no death comes,' she said; 'we use feasts that are lasting, and we do every kind thing without quarrelling; we are called the people of the Sídhe.' She was speaking to a high woman that death or old age would never come to — and she was asking Connla to come to Magh Mell, the Pleasant Plain, where he would be a king for ever without sorrow or fret, his body never withering from its youth.

The rest of the court heard every word and saw nobody; and Conn felt the raid in his own house: 'Help me, Coran, you that sing spells of the great arts. There is an attack made on me that is beyond my wisdom... an unseen figure fighting with me to bring away my beautiful son; the call of a woman is bringing him away from the hands of the king.' Coran the druid sang his counter-spells until her voice could not be heard and Connla could not see her any more — silencing as abduction. But driven off, she threw an apple to the prince; and for the length of a month Connla used no other food or drink, and for all he ate of it the apple grew no smaller. Hunger for the otherworld, in the literal sense.

At the month's end she returned, in Magh Archomnim, and this time the druid's law failed against her argument. 'It is a high place indeed Connla has among dying people, and death before him. But the Ever-Living Living Ones are asking you to take the sway over the people of Tethra.' When the king called again for Coran, she said the sentence that breaks the tale open: 'O Conn, fighter of a hundred, it is little love and little respect the wonderful tribes of Traig Mor, the Great Strand, have for Druids; and where its law comes, it scatters the spells on their lips.' The new age — the law that scatters spells — has arrived before her; the druids are already obsolete. Conn asked his son, and Connla gave the answer of every mortal in these tales: 'My own people are dearer to me than any other thing, yet sorrow has taken hold of me because of this woman.' She ended with the invitation no mortal refuses: 'Come now into my shining ship, if you will come to the Plain of Victory... There is no living race in it but women and girls only.' Connla made a leap from his people into the shining boat, and they watched him sail away in a mist as far as their eyes could reach. They have never come back, and only the gods know where they went. The echtra is the ancestor of every 'fairy lover' ballad — the call that arrives as a woman's voice the law cannot silence.
narrative.zh: 彼岸召喚中最短最冷的一篇：王之繼承人非失於戰爭，而是失於一句語法。百戰之王科恩之子紅髮科恩拉與父立於烏斯內克丘——愛爾蘭之臍——見一奇裝女子；惟彼可見。『我來自永生者之地提爾-南-貝歐，彼處無死亡；彼處宴飲不止、善事行之無爭；吾族稱西德之民。』她自稱是不老不死者，召科恩拉往宜人平原馬格·梅爾，彼處將永為王、無憂無慮、身體永不衰老。滿朝聞其聲而不見其人；科恩自覺家中有掠奪：『科蘭助我，你這誦大法咒語者。有不可見者與我爭鬥，欲奪我俊美之子；女子之呼正將他自王者之手帶走。』德魯伊科蘭誦反咒，直至其聲不可聞、科恩拉亦不能見她——以沉默行綁架。然被逐之女擲蘋果一枚予王子；一月之中，科恩拉不食他物，而蘋果食之不減——彼岸之饑渴，字面意義。月終她在馬格·阿爾科姆尼復至，此時德魯伊之法敗於其辯。『科恩拉在必死之民中位分誠高，死在其前。然永生者請你治理特特拉之民。』王再召德魯伊時，她說出撕裂全篇之句：『百戰科恩，大沙灘之奇妙諸族不甚愛德魯伊；其法所至，唇上咒語自散。』——新時代已先她而至，德魯伊已過時。王問其子，科恩拉答出此類故事中每個凡人之答：『吾族於我最親，然因此女子，悲傷已抓住我。』她以無人能拒之邀結束：『上我光輝之舟，同往勝利平原……其中生民惟女子與少女。』科恩拉自族人一躍入舟，眾人望其如霧中遠航至目力之極。彼等永不復返，惟神知其所往。此echtra乃一切『仙戀』敘事之祖——以法所不能禁之女聲而來之召喚。
